one_liner: Contract-less .NET binary serializer built on runtime-compiled Span/MemoryMarshal proxies; ~16x faster than protobuf-net and MessagePack-CSharp in its author's benchmark.
what_it_does: HyperSerializer turns a .NET object into bytes and back with no schema and no attributes: `HyperSerializer.Serialize(obj)` returns a `Span<byte>`, `HyperSerializer.Deserialize<T>(bytes)` reads it back, and there are `SerializeAsync`/`DeserializeAsync` variants over `Memory<byte>`. It writes the public fields and properties of a class, struct or value type in order, by position. Only `[IgnoreDataMember]` is honored. Supported member types are primitives, enums, Guid, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan, decimal, their nullables, strings, arrays of value types, and unmanaged structs. Nested class members and dictionaries are skipped silently. The README targets caching and messaging between services behind a firewall, where both ends share the same type layout.
how_it_is_fast: On the first use of each `T`, a static constructor reflects over the type and fills C# source templates to build a proxy class. It compiles that source at runtime with Roslyn (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp, Release optimization), loads the assembly, and caches the Serialize/Deserialize delegates in the static generic class `HyperSerializer<T>`. The generated code computes the exact output length (fixed member sizes plus string and array byte counts) and allocates one `byte[]`. It then writes each member as raw memory with `MemoryMarshal.Write` and reads it back with `MemoryMarshal.Read`. Strings are block-copied as UTF-16 through `MemoryMarshal.Cast<char,byte>`, and value-type arrays are block-copied too. The format has no field tags, no varints, no UTF-8 transcoding and no per-member type markers. Its only framing is a 1-byte null flag for each nullable and a 4-byte length prefix for each string or array.
when_to_use: Both ends run the same .NET 6-9 build (a shared DTO assembly) and exchange small, flat objects over a trusted link. The README names messaging between services behind a firewall as the target.
Short-lived caches of flat DTOs, in-process or remote, where you can flush the cache whenever a type changes.

Hot paths that serialize and deserialize one object at a time. The published run shows ~46 ns per round trip (derived: 46.24 ms / 1M) for a 10-member POCO with Guid, DateTime, decimal, TimeSpan, an enum and a string.

Bulk arrays of unmanaged structs, such as market ticks. Pass the whole `T[]` and it is stored as a length prefix plus one block copy (see test Test_Struct_Array_Should_Serialize and the author's advice in issue #8).
Types you cannot or will not annotate. No [ProtoContract], [MessagePackObject] or [Key] attributes are needed.
when_not_to_use: Persisted data, or services deployed on different schedules. The format is positional with no field IDs, so reordering, removing or retyping a member breaks reads. The README warns that mismatched bytes can decode into wrong values with no exception.

Any reader that is not .NET, or data exchanged across architectures. The bytes are raw CLR memory layout: Microsoft's docs say `MemoryMarshal.Write` copies private fields and implementation details. Byte order is the host's, strings are UTF-16, and no format spec exists.

Native AOT, trimmed or single-file apps. The library compiles C# with Roslyn at runtime, loads the result dynamically, and builds compiler references from `Assembly.Location`. Native AOT forbids dynamic loading, and single-file apps return an empty `Assembly.Location`.
Object graphs. Class-typed members and dictionaries are ignored, with no reference or cycle handling (issues #2 and #11), and a top-level `Dictionary<int,int>` throws (issue #1, open since 2022).

Processes where cold start or footprint matters. The first use of each type runs a Roslyn compilation, and the package depends on Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp. The repo does not document the compile cost.

integration.dependencies: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp >= 4.9.2 (Roslyn, used at runtime to compile the per-type proxies)
integration.platforms: Any OS/architecture running .NET 6-9 with JIT and runtime assembly loading. Native AOT is not supported, and single-file publish is likely incompatible. The wire format uses host byte order.
integration.thread_safety: The README claims 100% thread-safe. Per-type setup runs once in a static constructor, and the generated methods keep no shared state; each Serialize call allocates a new buffer. One exception: the struct-size cache in ReflectionExtensions.cs is a plain Dictionary that is read outside its lock during setup.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — types need no annotations, and each call site is one line. But the wire format is incompatible with protobuf and MessagePack, so both ends must switch together and existing stored data cannot be read.

gotchas: The async methods are synchronous wrappers, and `SerializeAsync` also copies the result with `ToArray()`. In issue #8, calling SerializeAsync per record into a MemoryStream took 1,967 ms, against 528 ms for TeaFiles, on 3.02M structs. The author's fix was the sync `Span` API, or serializing the whole array in one call.

Setup runs in the static constructor of `HyperSerializer<T>`, so codegen failures surface as TypeInitializationException (issues #1 and #4). The generated deserializer calls `new()` and assigns every scanned member, and MemberTypeInfo.cs never checks CanWrite. So types appear to need a public parameterless constructor and settable members. Set `HyperSerializerSettings` before the first use of each type.

Member order is public fields first, then properties, in reflection order. Microsoft documents that GetProperties order is unspecified on .NET 6 and earlier and deterministic from .NET 7. In the current source, setting `SerializeFields = false` keeps fields and drops properties, which is the opposite of what the README describes.

The README says generic lists work, but `TypeSupport` compares against the open generic `typeof(IEnumerable<>)`, which a `List<int>` never equals. So List members appear to be skipped silently, and the V3 test that covers lists uses a comparison helper that cannot return false. Value-type arrays do round-trip (issue #5 regression test). Struct members must not contain references, because `MemoryMarshal.Write` throws ArgumentException for those.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Bebop is the only sibling with a C# result. Pick HyperSerializer over Bebop when you want no .bop schema and no bebopc codegen step and both ends are the same .NET types. Pick Bebop when TypeScript, Rust or C++ must read the data. rkyv and Apache Fory (C++) are measured outside .NET, so they matter here only if you are not locked to .NET.
verified_claims_summary: The author's BenchmarkDotNet table (.NET 8.0.3 RyuJIT x64 AVX2, /p:Optimize=true, Intel Core i9-10980XE, Windows 11) shows 1M single-object serialize+deserialize round-trips of a 10-member POCO. HyperSerializer took 46.24 ms, against 98.81 ms for MemoryPack 1.9.16 (2.14x), 768.58 ms for MessagePack-CSharp 2.4.59 and 769.34 ms for protobuf-net 3.1.26 (both ~16.6x). Allocations were similar (~206 MB), except protobuf-net at 427 MB. The committed harness does not reproduce this exact table: its Test class has no string, and its loop and parameter setup differ. The '18x' and '3x vs Apex' figures come from an older chart with no environment listed.
status_note: Maintained but slow-moving. v1.6 (2025-11-05) only added net9.0; before it, the last code change was in April 2024. The repo has 85 stars, ~44k NuGet downloads and one open issue. Usable via NuGet under Apache-2.0 (the package ships an MIT License.txt), but its runtime Roslyn dependency rules out AOT and makes it heavier than its small source suggests.
